summary:
Amur Oblast stands under the national framework of Russia, where the UK government's country policy and information note of June 2025 records that same-sex sexual activity is not criminalised, while same-sex marriage and gender transition are banned and the Russian constitution offers no specific legal protections for LGBT+ people.

Legal gender recognition and gender-affirming care were prohibited outright in 2023, when the law signed by President Vladimir Putin banned gender reassignment surgery and the change of gender markers on official documents; trans-specific healthcare was effectively banned the same year. A trans visitor has no lawful route to have their documents recognised or amended in Russia and must travel on documents as issued.

Public expression 'promoting' non-heterosexual relationships or gender transition is punishable under the 'gay propaganda' law by fines or detention of up to 15 days, with repeated offences risking criminal prosecution and up to four years' imprisonment. Between 2022 and 2024 at least 139 people in Russia were affected by enforcement of anti-LGBT+ laws, including convictions, detentions and 'extremism' prosecutions.

The US State Department travel advisory for Russia warns all travellers of wrongful detention and arbitrary law enforcement, and notes that foreigners found guilty under the propaganda law face arrest, detention of up to 15 days and deportation. The advisory is Level 4, Do Not Travel, and carries warnings directed at LGBT travellers.

Human Rights Watch reported on 30 June 2025 that Russian courts have issued 101 'extremism'-related convictions for participating in the 'International LGBT Movement' or displaying its alleged symbols, and that 81 people in 98 court cases since January 2024 have been convicted of administrative offences for displaying those symbols, mostly on social media. These federal enforcement measures apply nationwide, Amur Oblast included.

The 2023 Supreme Court designation of the 'International LGBT Movement' as extremist enabled criminal prosecutions carrying up to 12 years in prison, building on the 2013 'gay propaganda' law. Within 48 hours of that ruling, masked police raided LGBTQ-friendly Moscow bars, where about 100 patrons at one venue were ordered to face walls, searched and photographed, while at least two other venues were raided the same night.

Physical coercion against transgender people is documented. BBC Russian (27 July 2024) followed "Ada", a transgender woman lured by relatives in summer 2021 to a conversion-therapy centre near Novosibirsk, where she was held for nine months and forced to take testosterone, pray and perform manual labour before escaping when police responded to a phone she had found.

In December 2024 the Associated Press reported that a Russian man detained on extremism-related charges over an LGBTQ+ travel agency was found dead in a pretrial detention facility. Arrests, club raids and extremism charges defined LGBTQ+ life in Russia through 2025, according to The Moscow Times (23 June 2025).

The UK Home Office country policy note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression affirms that LGBT+ people in Russia, including the autonomous republic of Chechnya, constitute a particular social group under the refugee convention, which sets the assessment standard for UK asylum claims.
tangentialFactors:
Enforcement is escalating in volume as well as severity. Meduza reported on 19 June 2025 that cases under Russia's propaganda laws have grown eighteenfold over the past decade, and that fines under those statutes brought more than 60 million rubles ($765,300) into the state budget in the two years preceding.

Human Rights Watch called on governments to offer safe haven to those fleeing Russia, and the UK country policy note treats LGBT+ Russians as a particular social group for refugee purposes, indicating that protection machinery abroad is attuned to the risks documented inside Russia.

The Moscow Times reported on 23 June 2025 that a St Petersburg queer woman described herself as "a second-class citizen" after the extremist designation, reflecting the social consequences of the legal regime alongside formal penalties.
localsOnly:
Residents of Amur Oblast face the same federal regime as the rest of Russia: gender transition and same-sex marriage are prohibited, trans-specific healthcare is effectively unavailable, and public expression of non-heterosexual relationships or gender transition carries fines or detention of up to 15 days, with repeat offences risking up to four years' imprisonment.

Between 2022 and 2024 at least 139 people across Russia were affected by enforcement of anti-LGBT+ laws, including convictions, detentions and 'extremism' prosecutions. Displaying alleged 'International LGBT Movement' symbols, mostly on social media, has produced 81 administrative convictions in 98 court cases since January 2024.

Participation in or display of symbols of the designated 'extremist' movement can be prosecuted criminally, carrying up to 12 years in prison.
outOfScopeNotes:
The inventory does not resolve whether Amur Oblast has recorded any 'extremism' convictions or administrative symbol-display cases of its own; the Human Rights Watch figures are national totals and are presented here as applying nationwide rather than as counts specific to the oblast.

No source in this inventory documents trans-specific violence, detention or police conduct within Amur Oblast itself; the documented incidents cited (the Moscow bar raids, the Novosibirsk conversion-therapy case, the pretrial detention death) occurred in other regions and are used to illustrate the national pattern.

The exact current wording and scope of the propaganda law as applied to gender transition, and whether any exemption exists for visitors travelling on documents that do not match their presentation, are not resolved by these sources.
